questions.q: Why did the lesson warn against over-selling the sealed-test gap to the naive baseline (25.1 vs 181.5)?
options: Naive is always better than a regression
Naive repeated a high promotion-week value for a whole quarter, so it looked unusually bad; the backtest average (95.7) is the stable comparison
The sealed test set was used to tune the naive model
The interval was too narrow
questions.explain: Naive's error varies a lot by window. Its backtest average was 95.7, so comparing against the backtest gives a fairer picture than one lucky-bad window.

questions.q: The 95% prediction interval covered 12 of 13 sealed weeks (92%). What is the right reading?
options: Proof that the interval is perfectly calibrated
Proof that the model is wrong
In line with the target, but 13 points are too few to certify calibration
It means the model must be re-tuned on the sealed weeks
questions.explain: 92% is consistent with 95%, but with only 13 points a single miss changes the coverage by about 8 points.

questions.q: What is the correct use of the sealed test set?
options: Score the final chosen model once, report the result, and do not change the model afterward
Test many models on it and keep the best one
Include it in the backtest so the model has more data
Tune hyperparameters against it
questions.explain: Repeated use of the test set leaks information from it into your choices, making the reported score optimistic.

questions.q: How should the week-8 promotion what-if (782 to about 1,025 units) be presented?
options: As a guaranteed outcome
As a model estimate that assumes the historical promotion lift holds; test it with a controlled experiment
As proof that promotions cause a 30% lift in every store
It should be hidden because what-if analyses are not allowed
questions.explain: The estimate comes from historical association. Promotions are rarely assigned at random, so a controlled test is the way to confirm the effect.

questions.q: Which is the best way to structure a short presentation of this project?
options: Start with the gradient boosting algorithm and finish with the code
Show only the model with the lowest error
Lead with the decision and baseline, then result and drivers in plain language, then the recommendation, then the limitations
Skip the limitations to keep it positive
questions.explain: Audiences care about the decision first. Stating limitations openly builds credibility.
